l: Theoclymenus’ palace, Hecuba and other plays
s: Theoclymenus’ palace is a splendid, wealthy royal residence in Pharos, belonging to Proteus and later ruled by his son. Proteus’ tomb stands at its entrance. Helen lives there under Proteus’ former protection while Theoclymenus seeks to marry her. Menelaus approaches for aid but is warned that Greeks are barred and endangered. Inside, Theonoe may reveal him, while Helen seeks servants’ help to escape.

l: Proteus's son, Hecuba and other plays
s: Proteus’s son rules Egypt after Proteus’s death, persecutes Helen to force marriage, and threatens hostile Greeks, making his palace dangerous to Menelaus.

l: the Chorus, Hecuba and other plays
s: supports justice [affirming the success of an honest cause] The Chorus supports the prophetic sentiments of the old man, prays for the prosperity of the race of Tantalus, and asks Theonoe to decide the matter in a way that pleases all. After Theonoe’s decision, it declares that impious men do not prosper and that honest causes have the fairest hopes.

Hermione is the daughter of Menelaus and Helen, a Spartan princess, queen, and wealthy wife of Achilles’ son, though she was formerly betrothed to Orestes. In her husband’s household, she regards Andromache as a rival and believes that Andromache has used drugs or magic to make her barren and hated. Defending what Menelaus calls her bridal rights, she confronts Andromache at Thetis’ temple, threatens her, and, with Menelaus’ help, seeks to kill both Andromache and her son Molossus; she is even given power to decide Molossus’ fate. Her actions reverse into extreme remorse when she fears punishment and exile from Phthia. Ashamed and terrified of her husband, she attempts suicide by noose or sword but is restrained. She asks Orestes to take her away and flees Peleus’ house, leaving behind a marriage Peleus curses.

l: cave containing Helen's phantom, Hecuba and other plays
s: contains Helen's phantom [under the guard of Menelaus’s companions] Menelaus hides the woman he believes to be Helen in a cave and leaves surviving companions to guard her. The phantom later leaves the cave and ascends into the heavens, revealing its true nature.

l: Menelaus's ship, Hecuba and other plays
s: Menelaus’s ship has been swallowed by the waves, leaving him without a vessel for escape. Helen therefore plans to obtain another ship under the pretext of casting Menelaus’s funeral trappings into the sea.

l: shipwreck of Menelaus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Menelaus’s ship is shattered on rocks, leaving only its keel; he and Helen’s phantom survive, while he reaches Egypt with few companions, tattered and without food, clothing, or royal possessions. Reported as drowned in a Libyan wreck, Menelaus uses the false account, supported by his appearance, for Helen’s funeral deception and escape plan.

l: Helen's abduction and substitution by an image, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_caused_by Juno [to rescue Helen from Venus] Helen was not taken to Troy or given to Paris; the son of Jove brought the real Helen to Egypt, while Juno substituted an etherial image for her. This deception caused the Trojan War and led Menelaus and the Greeks to suffer for an empty phantom.

l: prophecy and divination, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_unreliable false guidance [according to the messenger] Theonoe’s prophetic knowledge identifies Menelaus’s arrival and describes the conflict between Juno and Venus over his return. Her prophecy also presents the fictitious nature of Paris’s marriage to Helen and enables her to choose whether to expose or save Menelaus.

l: the sea, Hecuba and other plays
s: The sea has subjected Menelaus to years of wandering and shipwreck. Helen plans to claim that Menelaus died in the sea and to use the customs surrounding those who perish at sea to justify a funeral conducted without burial.

l: the swift car, Hecuba and other plays
s: Menelaus asks whether Helen can persuade one of the palace’s charioteers to provide a swift car. The plan does not develop further because their escape is instead organized around obtaining a ship.

l: the sword, Hecuba and other plays
s: Menelaus’s sword represents both his readiness to fight and the danger facing the couple. Helen says that the tomb and his drawn sword could protect him if the king tried to drag him away, and Menelaus threatens to use it to kill Helen and himself if necessary.

l: funeral trappings, Hecuba and other plays
s: Helen plans to place funeral trappings in a ship and cast them into the sea as though they belonged to Menelaus. Their presence will support the false report that he died in the shipwreck.

l: Helen’s escape from Egypt, Hecuba and other plays
s: Helen’s escape from Egypt is a planned flight with Menelaus. It depends on concealing Menelaus, falsely reporting that he died at sea, and obtaining permission and a vessel for his funeral rites. Helen and Menelaus board the funeral ship with surviving sailors, who arm themselves; Menelaus leads it, they defeat Theoclymenus’s sailors, seize control, and flee Egypt.

l: the false funeral, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_planned_by Helen [as a deception to obtain a ship] The false funeral is intended to persuade the king that Menelaus has died in the sea. Helen will cut her hair, put on mourning clothes, feign grief, request a ship for the funeral rites, and use the ceremony to escape with Menelaus.

l: the Greek sailors, Hecuba and other plays
s: serve Theoclymenus [Egyptian sailors aboard the Sidonian ship] The Greek sailors pretend to be shipwrecked survivors and board the Sidonian ship with the funeral gifts. They take up arms when Menelaus gives the signal, defeat the Egyptian sailors, and help sail the ship toward Greece.

l: Tyrian bark, Hecuba and other plays
s: has_capacity fifty oars [provided for the funeral voyage] Theoclymenus orders a Tyrian bark with fifty oars and skilled sailors for the supposed funeral rites. Helen ensures that the sailors understand that Menelaus is to direct the ship.

l: the funeral rites of Menelaus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Menelaus's funeral rites are a claimed Greek ceremony for one drowned: an empty garment is buried and offerings cast into the sea, including blood, animals, arms, flowers, a bier, ship, and sailors.

l: Paris’s abduction of Helen, Hecuba and other plays
s: Paris is said to have carried Helen from hospitable shores to Priam’s realm, relying on barbaric oars and pursuing a marriage led by Venus. His act is presented as the cause of the war and Troy’s ruin.

l: marriage of Helen and Theoclymenus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Theoclymenus intends to marry Helen and believes that she has finally accepted him after Menelaus’s supposed death. He orders bridal gifts and plans a public celebration, but Helen only pretends to consent in order to escape.

l: false report of Menelaus’s death, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_reported_by Theonoe [to Helen and Theoclymenus] Helen says that Theonoe and a mariner reported Menelaus’s death at sea. The report is deliberately used to gain Theoclymenus’s cooperation in the funeral and to conceal Menelaus’s presence.

l: marriage and fidelity, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_exemplified_by Helen [her continued love for Menelaus] Helen presents herself as faithful to Menelaus, saying that she retains the memory of their marriage and will honor him even after his supposed death. She tells Theoclymenus that she has practiced loving her friends, while secretly remaining devoted to Menelaus and escaping with him.

l: the Dioscuri, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Dioscuri are Castor and Pollux, divine brothers and Helen’s protectors. They prevent Theoclymenus from killing Theonoe, explain Helen’s fate, guide Helen and Menelaus, and announce future divine honors.

l: the palace, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_located_in Egypt [the royal residence] The palace is where the Messenger discovers that Helen has departed. It is also the place from which Helen is escorted toward the harbor under the pretense that she is mourning Menelaus.

l: the Sidonian ship, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Sidonian ship, a large vessel with fifty oars, is equipped and boarded by Menelaus’s party, which defeats its Egyptian sailors and takes it toward Greece.

l: Menelaus’s deception, Hecuba and other plays
s: involves the funeral rites of Menelaus [a false funeral was used to board the ship] Menelaus deceives Theoclymenus by pretending to be dead and presenting the voyage as a funeral rite for an empty tomb. He also uses shipwrecked clothing and a false account to bring his Greek companions aboard.

l: the sea battle aboard the ship, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_fought_between the Greek sailors [the sailors fight the Greek rescuers] The sea battle begins when Menelaus kills the bull and orders the Greeks to attack the Egyptians. Swords and oars are used in the confined space, many men are killed or thrown into the waves, and Menelaus’s party takes the ship.
A female slave formerly serving Andromache in Ilium, she loyally warns Andromache of Hermione and Menelaus’s plot to kill her son and offers to seek Peleus’s help despite danger.

l: Chorus of Phthian women, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Chorus of Phthian women, a group native to Phthia, shares Andromache’s troubles while fearing Hermione and the rulers. Remaining at home, it guards absent friends’ fortunes, counsels Andromache to act mildly, links present grief to Troy’s destruction, reports Hermione’s flight and Orestes’ threat, mourns the dead youth and Peleus, and ends by seeing divine guidance in human affairs.

Molossus is the infant son of Andromache, linked to Neoptolemus and a Trojan lineage. Secretly brought from Thetis’s altar, he is threatened and condemned to die with Andromache for her alleged offense, though he pleads for mercy. Peleus declares him faultless, frees him from chains, and promises to educate him in Phthia.

l: Nurse of Hermione, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hermione’s old friend and attendant protects her from suicide, urging her inside, predicting pardon and support, and warning her not to appear outside.

Orestes, son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, is Hermione’s kinsman and former betrothed. He murders his mother, then seeks Hermione while traveling to Dodona. Jealous of her husband, Achilles’ son, he plots and engineers his death at Delphi through accusations, calumny, and stratagem.

is_a sacred city [the city of Apollo’s oracle] Delphi is the sacred realm and city where Achilles’ son is ambushed and killed. Thetis commands Peleus to return the body there so that its tomb will proclaim the violence committed by Orestes’ band.

l: Thetis’ temple, Hecuba and other plays
s: Thetis’ temple between Phthia and Pharsalia commemorates her marriage to Peleus and becomes Andromache’s sacred asylum against Hermione’s threat.

l: altar of Thetis, Hecuba and other plays
s: The altar of Thetis is a hallowed sanctuary where Andromache and Molossus seek asylum. Though it offers protection, Hermione says neither altar nor temple will save Andromache, and Menelaus forces her from it before ordering her seizure.

l: marriage of Thetis and Peleus, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a divine-human marriage [a source of both descendants and calamity] Thetis recalls the ties of her marriage with Peleus and presents his having married a goddess as a blessing. Peleus says that a prudent man should choose a nobly born consort and marry his daughters into virtuous families rather than rely on wealth.

Jealousy drives Hermione’s hostility toward Andromache. Andromache says that Hermione’s hatred comes from jealous love and from her inability to live harmoniously with her husband, rather than from magic drugs.

l: magic drugs, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hermione accuses Andromache of secretly using magic drugs to make her barren and hateful to Neoptolemus. Andromache denies the charge and says that Hermione’s husband dislikes her because of her character and conduct.

l: female virtue and domestic harmony, Hecuba and other plays
s: wins a husband’s love [according to Andromache] Andromache argues that female virtue, modesty, patience, and willingness to yield bring affection and domestic harmony. She contrasts her own conduct toward Hector with Hermione’s jealousy, pride, and desire to dominate her husband.

l: barbarian customs, Hecuba and other plays
s: include family sexual relations [as alleged by Hermione] Hermione claims that barbarian peoples permit incest, murder among relatives, and other unlawful conduct. Andromache rejects the contrast as unfair, saying that both Phrygia and Greece condemn base actions.

l: Andromache’s enslavement, Hecuba and other plays
s: After Troy’s defeat and destruction, Andromache is forcibly taken from Troy aboard the Argive fleet to Phthia, where she must live with Hector’s killers.

l: Hermione’s marriage, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hermione’s marriage is a bridal union whose rights Menelaus defends during her husband's absence. Her father first betrothed her to Orestes, then promised her to Achilles’ son, who married her after Troy but loves captive rival Andromache; Andromache predicts Hermione's rejection.

l: execution of Andromache and Molossus, Hecuba and other plays
s: The execution of Andromache and Molossus is a death sentence imposed by Menelaus and Hermione: Menelaus condemns Andromache and Hermione condemns Molossus. Menelaus orders them sent together to the underworld while Neoptolemus is absent, but Peleus frees and shelters them, preventing the killings; Hermione later confesses and grieves.

l: marital conflict and polygamy, Hecuba and other plays
s: causes connubial woe [when rival consorts or sons by different mothers exist] The Chorus declares that rival consorts and sons born to different mothers fill a household with strife and banish conjugal love. It compares divided marriage to divided rule, saying that conflict arises when two wives or two rulers share authority.

l: chains binding Andromache and Molossus, Hecuba and other plays
s: The chains bind Andromache and Molossus while they are being taken to execution. Peleus orders that they be removed, and he personally frees them after rebuking Menelaus for treating Andromache as though she were a trapped animal.

l: marriage of Neoptolemus and Andromache, Hecuba and other plays
s: Neoptolemus and Andromache form an alliance through marriage; she is bestowed as a reward for his valor, then Menelaus challenges her place while Peleus defends it.

l: inheritance and legitimate rule, Hecuba and other plays
s: concerns Phthia [whether barbarian sons may rule Greek land] Menelaus argues that Andromache's sons, as children of a barbarian woman, should not rule Phthia if his daughter has no child. Peleus and Menelaus dispute whether descent, marriage, and legitimacy should determine who inherits and rules.

l: justice and vengeance, Hecuba and other plays
s: Peleus condemns Menelaus for allowing execution to outstrip righteous judgment and for using murderous violence against Andromache and Molossus. Menelaus claims that he is bound to avenge the wrongs done to his daughter and promises that Neoptolemus will experience treatment corresponding to his deeds.

l: nobility and virtue, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_not_limited_by legitimate birth [virtue may appear in bastards] The Chorus praises descent from generous sires, inherited honors, and virtue whose memory survives death. Peleus argues that true worth consists in courage and honest zeal rather than high position, wealth, or inherited reputation.

l: bastardy and legitimacy, Hecuba and other plays
s: Peleus says that a bastard may possess greater virtue than someone lawfully born and compares good character to fertile soil rather than legal birth. Menelaus nevertheless objects that Andromache's sons, born from a barbarian mother, should not rule Greeks.

l: female chastity and adultery, Hecuba and other plays
s: Peleus condemns Helen as adulterous and blames Menelaus for leaving his house unguarded and later sparing her. He also attacks Spartan customs, claiming that women educated in athletic freedom may become unchaste, while Menelaus argues that Helen's suffering was imposed by the gods.

is_a group of women [sympathetic to Hermione] The Chorus confirms that Hermione is attempting to die and urges her not to act violently against herself. It rebukes Hermione for condemning all women and sings of Troy’s destruction, the deaths of its rulers, and the suffering caused by the Trojan War.

l: Andromache’s young son, Hecuba and other plays
s: Andromache’s young son, the only surviving royal branch of Aeacus, lives with Andromache in Molossia and founds a future line of ruling descendants.

l: Hermione’s bridal mansion, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_the_residence_of Hermione [as queen and wife] Hermione’s bridal mansion is the household where she lives with Achilles’ son and where she attempts suicide. She fears that Achilles’ son will return there, kill her, or force her to become the slave of Andromache.

l: Hermione’s attempted suicide, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_caused_by remorse [after the attempted murder] Hermione attempts to kill herself by hanging herself with a noose or stabbing herself with a sword. The Nurse and servants stop her, and she later asks Orestes to rescue her from the consequences of her actions.

l: death plot against Achilles’ son, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_prepared_by Orestes [with artifice and armed supporters] Orestes says that he has arranged an unavoidable death plot against Achilles’ son with armed allies stationed in the Pythian realm. He intends to present the deed as an exploit at Delphi and claims that Apollo will bring vengeance upon Achilles’ son.

reports Neoptolemus’s murder at Delphi [to Peleus and his friends] The Messenger reports that Achilles’ son was killed by Delphi’s citizens and Orestes. He describes the ambush at Apollo’s temple, Achilles’ son’s resistance, his eventual slaughter, and the return of his body to Peleus.

l: Delphi’s citizens, Hecuba and other plays
s: Delphi’s citizens, persuaded by Orestes’ accusations, defend Apollo’s temple by ambushing Achilles’ son, pelting him with stones and weapons, and killing him.

is_ruled_by Andromache’s young son [through his future royal descendants] Molossia is the land where Thetis orders Andromache and her young son to live. The young son’s descendants are destined to rule there as a succession of happy kings.

l: Sepia cave, Hecuba and other plays
s: Thetis tells Peleus to keep his station in the cave that time has worn through the rock of Sepia. She will later come with the Nereids to carry him away.

l: Apollo’s temple at Delphi, Hecuba and other plays
s: Apollo’s temple at Delphi, an unpolluted sanctuary with holy treasures, hosts Orestes’ ambush; Achilles’ son seeks atonement, then citizens kill him beside altar.

l: Neoptolemus’s murder at Delphi, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_committed_by Delphi’s citizens [with Orestes as contriver] The murder of Achilles’ son at Delphi is carried out by a Delphian with the help of a multitude after Orestes has turned the citizens against him. His body is covered with wounds and cast from the temple before being taken to Peleus.

l: Neoptolemus’s burial, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_ordered_by Thetis [at Apollo’s altar in Delphi] Thetis orders Achilles’ son’s body to be taken back to Delphi and buried there. His tomb is to testify to the murderous violence committed by Orestes’ band.

l: Peleus’s apotheosis, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_granted_by Thetis [as an immortal and incorruptible existence] Thetis promises to release Peleus from human suffering by making him immortal and incorruptible. He will live with her as a god in Nereus’s watery dwelling and later behold Achilles.

Euripides’ Medea is a tragedy centered on the collapse of Medea and Jason’s relationship and on Medea’s transformation from abandoned wife into avenger. Medea, a princess and enchantress from Colchis, once helped Jason and the Argonauts, left her family and homeland for him, and bore him two children in Greece. Now Jason plans to marry Creon’s daughter, a Corinthian princess, claiming the match will bring security and royal connections. Medea sees it as betrayal and as proof of women’s dependence and vulnerability in marriage and exile. The Nurse, Attendant, and Corinthian women fear Medea’s grief and anger. Creon orders Medea and her children expelled, but she gains one day’s delay. She vows that the princess, Creon, and Jason will die, yet needs a place of refuge. When Aegeus, king of Athens, promises her protection, she can pursue revenge without fear of having nowhere to go. Medea pretends to reconcile with Jason and sends her children to the royal bride with a poisoned robe and golden carcanet. Jason accepts the apparent reconciliation and hopes the children may remain in Corinth. The gifts kill both the princess and Creon. Medea then faces the conflict between love for her children and the desire to wound Jason completely. Despite the Chorus’s horror and the children’s cries, she kills them. Jason arrives after the deaths. Medea appears above him in a winged-dragon chariot, holding the children’s bodies and denying him burial rites. She declares her vengeance complete; Jason is left grieving, childless, and unable to repair the destruction.

Medea is a tragedy of character and situation, first produced in Athens in 432 B.C. Its concentrated, passionate action examines the end of Medea and Jason’s romance through oppression and revenge, as Medea becomes the instrument of judgment against Jason. It received third prize at its first production.

Medea is a woman, princess and enchantress of Colchis, daughter of Aietes and of an old king, descended from the Sun through her father, and allied with Hecate. Skilled in unknown and evil lore, she is also a wife, mother, and foreign, landless woman. Her total devotion to Jason leads her to rescue him in the quest for the Golden Fleece, kill its guarding serpent, betray her father, leave her homeland, and help cause Pelias's death. She becomes Jason's wife and bears their two children. When Jason abandons her to marry Creon's daughter, Medea is condemned to exile from Corinth. Devastated, she curses Jason, the bride, and their house; her injuries turn her into a living Curse. She gains one remaining day from Creon, rejects Jason's assistance, and obtains Aegeus's oath of refuge in Athens. Determined on revenge against Jason, his new bride, and her father, she considers poison and fire, invokes Hecate, and chooses poisoned gifts. Though she loves her children and hesitates in grief, she sends them with the gifts, learns that the princess and king have died, and kills the children with a sword so that her enemies cannot seize them. She escapes in a winged-dragon chariot received through her divine lineage, refuses Jason access to the bodies, and travels to Pallas' plain. Within the tragic judgment, she becomes a dea ex machina while remaining subject to vengeance for the killings.

Jason is Aeson’s son, Pelias’s nephew, and the kingly heir of Iolcos in Thessaly. A famous, ambitious Greek hero and chief of the Argonauts, he seeks the Golden Ram’s fleece and ancestral honour, accepting Medea’s help and flight from Colchis. He becomes Medea’s husband and the father of their two children, though the introduction says their marriage is not legal. Later, valuing political security, prosperity, and career above love, he abandons Medea and their sons to marry Creon’s daughter, a royal bride. Medea, the Nurse, and the Attendant condemn this as betrayal; Medea calls him evil and a thief and blames his new marriage for her exile. Jason defends himself by claiming her curses caused the exile and that his marriage will secure a prosperous household and future for the children. He offers Medea money and support, which she rejects. When she appears reconciled, he agrees to protect the children and let them bring gifts to his bride. After Medea kills the bride, the king, and their children, Jason arrives to save the sons, learns they are dead, curses Medea, grieves his childlessness, and is denied their burial.

Euripides is a poet, sceptic, and devotee of truth. In the early preserved Medea, his youthful, austere, passionate realism exposes tragedy beneath heroic romance, repeatedly examining oppression, revenge, and cruelty’s damage to victims and avengers.

Creon is the ruler and king of Corinth, father of the princess who is to marry Jason. Fearing Medea will harm his daughter, Jason, or himself, he orders Medea and her two children into exile, yet grants them one final day in Corinth under threat of death after sunrise. As the bride’s father and one of Medea’s intended victims, he is caught in her revenge: he finds and embraces his dead daughter, is trapped by her poisoned robes, and dies with her.

Aegeus, Pandion’s son and king of Athens, is a childless man praised as gentle and righteous. Returning from Delphi after praying for children, he meets Medea, seeks her promised magic, and grants her refuge in Athens, swearing by Earth, the Sun, and the gods to protect her while he lives and is free.
Colchis is Aietes’ distant land and Medea’s homeland, Jason’s destination for the Golden Ram’s fleece and Phrixus’s soul, before Medea betrays and leaves it.

Corinth is a city ruled by Creon. After the catastrophe at Iolcos, Jason brings Medea there, where they live with their children. Jason is to marry Creon’s daughter, and the royal bride’s household is there. Creon treats Medea as a dangerous foreigner and orders her and the children beyond the city’s borders. For Jason, Corinth represents orderly life under justice and law; for Medea, it becomes the place of rejection, ruin, and exile.
Athens is a walled hill ruled by Aegeus. It matters as Medea’s intended refuge: Aegeus promises her a home, protection, and safety from seizure once she reaches Attic earth.
Argo, the first ship, is built for Jason’s expedition to Colchis, recalls his heroic romantic past, then rots where it stands.
The Argonauts are heroes gathered from across Hellas to accompany Jason aboard Argo on the quest for the Golden Ram; Medea helps them survive and counsels them home.

has wildness and beauty [throughout Greek literature] The Argo legend is described as wild and beautiful and as running through Greek literature from early Corinthian lays to Pindar and Apollonius Rhodius. Euripides draws on this legendary material but looks past its enchantment to the tragedy beneath it.

The romance between Jason and Medea is treated as something whose ending is the reverse of its earlier enchantment. The introduction argues that most romances contain a flaw, and that the flaw in this one is fatal because Jason’s ambition and Medea’s destructive devotion make their relationship incapable of lasting.

The tragedy of Medea is rooted in the collision between Jason’s pursuit of status and Medea’s betrayed love. Its dramatic power comes from showing oppression turning the victim into an agent of further cruelty rather than into a figure of morally triumphant virtue.

Love is a bond between man and woman, powerful, transitory, irrational, and potentially disturbing. It can bless through gentleness, yet can turn poisonous, producing hatred, strife, destructive desire, and suffering. Medea’s love for Jason makes her help and kill for him, abandon her family, and expect perfect devotion in return. Jason’s new love weakens their bond; his rejection shatters Medea’s world and turns her devotion into hatred, showing its destructive intensity.

Oppression and revenge form a recurring Euripidean dramatic pattern discussed in the introduction. Euripides shows that cruelty not only causes suffering but can make the victim worse, so the eventual revenge no longer appears as a triumph of justice.

Vengeance in the Medea is a powerful yet morally and emotionally unsatisfying force. Born from Medea’s injuries and cruelty’s pain, it kills the princess, king, and children, worsens Jason’s suffering, threatens him after the killings, and leaves him lonely while Medea escapes.

Medea's elderly, trusted nurse guards Jason and Medea's children, recounts Medea's history with Jason, fears her enraged revenge against herself, Jason, the bridegroom, or the king, and keeps the children away while seeking the Chorus's understanding.

l: the two children of Jason and Medea, Medea
s: The entity is the two sons of Medea and Jason. They are ordered into exile from Corinth with Medea and face a threat of death if they remain after the appointed day. Jason says his new marriage was intended to secure their future and connect them with royal children, while Medea refuses his aid. During her feigned reconciliation, they greet Jason, are said to be spared exile, and carry Medea’s robe and golden carcanet to the royal bride. Unaware of Medea’s distress, they later return, are sent inside, and are killed by Medea. Their bodies leave with her in the winged-dragon chariot, beyond Jason’s reach.

l: the Chorus of Corinthian Women, Medea
s: The Chorus of Corinthian Women is a collective singing group of women, divided into speaking groups, that responds to Medea’s suffering and deeds. It first comes after hearing her cries, sympathizes with her, and promises secrecy, while fearing for the innocent children. It judges the hatred between Medea and Jason as terrible, laments women’s wrongs and abandonment, and declares that life, laws, marriage, and gender relations will be transformed. After celebrating Athens and Aegeus, it urges Medea not to kill the children, foresees the royal bride’s death, and mourns the children’s fate. After the deaths, it reacts with horror and pity, condemns Medea’s killing of her children, warns Jason of coming wrath, and some women try to save the children.

is_a house [in Corinth and occupied by Medea] Medea's house is the place where she lies fasting and grieving after Jason's betrayal. The Nurse fears that Medea may die there or use a blade against Jason, and Medea later comes out of the house to address the Corinthian women.

l: the oath between Medea and Jason, Medea
s: A sworn marriage-and-loyalty bond between Medea and Jason, recalled by Medea after Jason breaks faith; she invokes Zeus and Themis as witnesses and seeks its end.

l: the marriage of Jason and Creon's daughter, Medea
s: Jason's new marriage to Creon's daughter, arranged by Creon, causes Medea's abandonment and grief; Creon protects his daughter, while Medea curses the bride and pretends acceptance to gain access for revenge.

Medea’s exile is a one-day, swift banishment from Corinth, ordered by Creon under royal authority and imposed through Jason. Creon commands Medea and her two children to leave and never return. Medea accepts but gains a day to seek counsel and comfort the children. Facing loss of home and feared hostility after the murders, she refuses Jason’s aid, secures Aegeus’s refuge in Athens, and tries unsuccessfully to keep the children from being separated from her.

Medea’s revenge is a planned retaliation for Jason’s betrayal and her exile. She confides in Corinthian women, demands secrecy, and warns of a wronged woman’s violence. It unfolds as a plan to kill Jason’s new bride and their children, leaving Jason childless and devastated.

afflicts Medea [through Jason's abandonment] Jason's abandonment of Medea is presented as a betrayal of their marriage, shared history, and oath. Medea describes herself as cast aside after leaving her father's home and land for Jason.

is_a burden [imposed on women by social and marital dependence] Medea says that women must pay for marriage, accept a master of their bodies, and learn how to live peacefully with a husband in unfamiliar laws and places. She argues that women remain bound to one person while men can leave home for other pleasures, and that bearing children is a greater burden than facing battle three times.

is_exercised_by Creon [as ruler of the land] Creon exercises Corinthian royal authority by ordering Medea and the children into exile and threatening them with death if they disobey. He describes the decree as his judgment and says that neither Medea's words nor her arts can overturn it.

Jason's new bride is a maiden princess, daughter of Creon, the king and ruler of Corinth, and queen in Jason's nearer house through his political remarriage. Her elevation above Medea makes her a target of Medea's curse and planned killings. She accepts the robes and golden crown delivered by Medea's children, an act that spares the children from exile. The poisoned gifts burn her in agony, killing her before her father arrives.

l: the women of the Chorus, Medea
s: A group of women sympathizes with Medea as displaced and landless, condemns men’s wrongs against women, and sings of her sea-crossing, broken oath, and loss of both paternal home and promised household.

is_a bridal feast [associated with darkness and suffering] Medea vows that the bride and groom's wedding feast and the day on which they joined hands will be dark. The wedding is presented as the event that accompanies Medea's rejection and expulsion.
Medea plans to kill Jason, the bride, and the bride's father, weighing fire, stabbing, or poison before resolving to kill them even if she must die afterward.

is_a murder_method [preferred by Medea] Medea intends the poison to be contained in the robe and crown given to the royal bride. She says that the poison will kill the bride and anyone who touches her in her agony.

are_transformed by Medea's actions [according to the Chorus] Marriage is shown as a structure in which the new bride becomes more valued and Medea is displaced and hunted away. The Chorus argues that women may become powerful figures in story, while men may become fearful and low, reversing familiar accounts of gender.

causes the exile of Medea and her children Jason has taken another wife, the daughter of the ruler of Corinth, after abandoning Medea despite her sacrifices and their children. He defends the remarriage as a way to gain prosperity, royal connections, and a stronger future for the children, while Medea calls it a violation of sworn faith.

occurs_during the quest for the Golden Fleece [aboard the Argo] Medea says that she saved Jason by helping him yoke the fiery bulls, sow the field of the Lords of Death, kill the sleepless serpent guarding the Golden Fleece, and escape with the prize. She also says that she left her father and home and caused Pelias's death for Jason's sake.

is_a childlessness [a lifelong source of sorrow] Aegeus tells Medea that he is childless because the god has willed it so, and that he has sought an answer from Apollo at Delphi. Medea promises that she knows magical herbs and will make him a father, and this promise helps move him to protect her.

is_a condition of being without a city [especially for Medea] Medea describes exile as being cast out helpless and alone, without a fatherland, home, brother, or city to shelter her. The Chorus likewise laments the fate of a woman driven from her father's home and forced onto a difficult road.

l: the killing of the royal bride, Medea
s: Medea plans to kill the royal bride by sending her a robe and a golden carcanet treated with poison. The Chorus later reports that the bride has accepted the gifts and is doomed.

l: the killing of Medea's children, Medea
s: The killing of Medea's sons by their mother is perpetrated by Medea with a sword. She resolves to kill her children to wound Jason and deny her enemies mockery, briefly hesitates, then sends them inside and kills them. Their cries are heard outside, leaving Jason broken and childless.

Poisoned gifts are fine bridal robes and a gold wreath or crown sent by Medea through her children to Jason’s bride, the princess. Offered as marriage gifts, they are identified as instruments of her death: the crown becomes consuming fire, the robes burn her flesh, and the king dies when he embraces her.

The Messenger warns Medea to flee because the princess and the king have been killed by her poison. He describes how the princess's golden crown and fine robes burned her flesh and how the king died while embracing her.
The winged-dragon chariot carries Medea above the house with the bodies of her children. Medea says that her father's father, the Sun, sent it to save her from her enemies.
Medea calls on her right hand to take up the sword when she prepares to kill her children. One of the children later cries that she has almost caught him and has a sword.

l: the murder of the princess and king, Medea
s: Medea’s poisoned gifts murder the princess with burning crown and robes; the king dies clinging to her body.

Medea says that Jason's false wooing, betrayal, and new marriage were part of the wrongs that led to the deaths. Jason describes Medea as a wife who has made him suffer, while Medea declares that neither Jason nor the princess was destined to live a happy married life.

The document contains summaries of two tragedies, HIPPOLYTUS and THE BACCHAE, each centered on a god’s punishment of mortals who reject or dishonor divine power. In HIPPOLYTUS, Aphrodite resolves to punish Hippolytus because he honors Artemis and refuses Aphrodite. Phaedra, Hippolytus’s stepmother, wastes away from a secret, unwanted love for him. After the Nurse draws out and then betrays Phaedra’s secret, Hippolytus angrily rejects the accusation and swears silence. Phaedra hangs herself but leaves a tablet that makes Theseus believe Hippolytus violated her. Theseus curses and exiles his son; Hippolytus is then fatally injured when a supernatural Sea-Bull terrifies his horses and wrecks his chariot. Artemis reveals Phaedra’s false accusation and Aphrodite’s role. Hippolytus forgives Theseus before dying, and Artemis promises him lasting honors and vengeance against Cypris. In THE BACCHAE, Dionysus arrives at Thebes to establish his worship, vindicate Semelê, and punish those, including Pentheus, who deny his divinity. He has driven the women of Thebes, including Agave, into ecstatic mountain worship. Cadmus and Teiresias support Dionysus, but Pentheus condemns the rites, arrests the stranger who is Dionysus, and resists repeated warnings. Dionysus escapes imprisonment, while reports show the Bacchae performing wonders and violent acts. He then deceives Pentheus into dressing as a woman to spy on the worshippers on Kithaeron. There, Dionysus causes Agave, Ino, Autonoë, and the Maenads to kill Pentheus. Agave returns carrying her son’s head, believing it a lion’s, until Cadmus forces her to recognize the truth. Dionysus declares the catastrophe punishment for rejected divinity and foretells exile and transformation for Cadmus and his family. Both works end in grief, ruined households, and reflections on divine justice exceeding human understanding.

Cypris is the Cyprian Queen, a powerful goddess of love whose home is Cyprus, especially Paphos, and whose visible cult image is the statue of Aphrodite. She blesses pious hearts and those who honor her, but punishes resistance and seeks human praise. Hippolytus holds her least among spirits, rejects her worship for Artemis, and maintains chastity; Cypris hates this defiance. She causes Love and makes Phaedra love Hippolytus, intending that her passion lead Theseus to curse and destroy him. Her rancor ultimately brings Phaedra’s and Hippolytus’s deaths and Theseus’s ruin.

Theseus is king of Athens and Trozên, husband of Phaedra, father of Hippolytus, and son of Poseidon. Granted three prayers by Poseidon, he returns to find Phaedra dead and reads her accusation against Hippolytus. Without investigation, grief and rage lead him to reject Hippolytus’s oath, curse him through Poseidon’s power, and exile him. When Hippolytus dies, Theseus first believes the punishment justified. Artemis reveals Phaedra’s lie and Hippolytus’s innocence; Theseus repents, is forgiven by his dying son, and mourns him. He also undergoes exile for bloodshed among kinsmen.

Phaedra is a Cretan princess, daughter of Minos, queen and wife of Theseus, mother of children, and a woman in Troezen whose deepest concern is honour amid shame. Overwhelmed by a forbidden, grievous love for Hippolytus, said to come through Cypris, she becomes ill, fasts, and hides her inward grief. She first tries silence and endurance, but after the Nurse reveals her secret and Hippolytus rejects it, she chooses death to protect her honour, her children, and the Cretan house. She hangs herself and leaves a tablet, a false written accusation that Theseus treats as proof against Hippolytus. Artemis says Phaedra resisted the imposed love until the betrayal, then wrote the accusation and died.

Hippolytus is a prince, son of Theseus and Hippolyte, reared strictly by Pittheus. Devoted above all to Artemis, whom he serves and who loves him, he values chastity, purity, hunting, and a life apart from sexual desire. He rejects Aphrodite, hates Love and women as sources of corruption, and returns from hunting to praise Artemis with a garland from an untouched meadow. After overhearing the Nurse's disclosure, he reacts with horror but keeps his oath of silence. When Phaedra dies and accuses him through her tablet, he protests his innocence yet will not break that oath. Theseus exiles and curses him through Poseidon. His horses panic at a supernatural Sea-Bull, wrecking his chariot and fatally injuring him. Before dying, he learns the truth, forgives Theseus, and is later honored in Trozên.

Artemis is a virgin goddess, daughter of Zeus and Leto and sister of Apollo. Praised by Hippolytus and hunters, she is associated with hunting, chastity, and companionship in the chase. She favors and loves Hippolytus, while opposing Cypris. After Hippolytus is driven away and prays before her statue, Artemis appears, proves his innocence, exposes Phaedra’s false accusation and Cypris’s part in the disaster, comforts him, grants him lasting funeral honors in Trozên, and vows vengeance.

l: the Nurse of Phaedra, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: The Nurse of Phaedra is Phaedra’s handmaid, watcher, and caregiver from youth, loving her as mistress and child. Seeking to relieve Phaedra’s illness, she presses her to confess love for Hippolytus, blames Aphrodite, and argues surrender to Cypris is wiser than resistance. She offers love-philtres and breaks her oath by seeking a word from Hippolytus, who condemns her; Phaedra curses and dismisses her.

Zeus, Semelê’s divine partner and Dionysus’s father, saves the unborn Dionysus from the fire that kills Semelê, devises a secret birth, and protects the child from Hera with a likeness made from a fragment of the world-encircling fire.

Dionysus is a god, child and true son of Zeus and Semelê, born from Semelê after her death by lightning and protected by Zeus. Known as Bromios and lord to his worshippers, he bears the ivy-bound thyrsus, wears fawn-skin, is crowned with ivy, and is linked with the clustered vine, wine, prophecy through frenzy, forgetting, release from care, armies, and ecstatic worship. He has taught and revealed his rites and mysteries throughout Asia and other lands, gathering chosen followers and wild women before coming to Thebes disguised as a mortal. There he seeks recognition of his godhead, vindication for Semelê, and establishment of his worship, while Pentheus blasphemously denies him and wages war against him. Captured, bound, shorn, and imprisoned, Dionysus stays calm, says the god will free him, frees the Maids, and escapes by divine power while Pentheus strikes an illusion. He warns Pentheus, then leads him into spying on the Bacchae at Kithaeron, declaring his doom. Dionysus directs the Maenads against Pentheus and finally tells Cadmus and Agave that their suffering punishes their mockery and denial of his divinity, while announcing their family’s future fate.

l: the Trozenian women, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: The Trozenian women are a chorus of fifteen women of Trozên, dwelling in Pelops’ land. They gather outside the castle to seek the cause of Phaedra’s wasting illness, question the Nurse, love Phaedra sympathetically, and swear silence about her griefs. They praise her virtue, sing of Erôs and Cypris’s destructive power, and foresee her hanging. After witnessing Phaedra’s death, Theseus’s accusation, and Hippolytus’s exile, they lament ruined royalty, wrongdoing, uncertain divine justice, Hippolytus’s suffering, and the people’s grief after his death.

Trozên is the play’s setting, Pelops’ land, and Hippolytus’s beloved youthful home, with a broad plain and surrounding mountains, springs, woods, and shore. There, after Theseus’s exile, Phaedra and Theseus reside; Trozên’s daughters witness Phaedra’s illness and keep her secret. Hippolytus rejects Aphrodite, bids Trozên farewell, is destroyed and carried there after the wreck, and is honored through rites, songs, and maidens’ hair-cutting.
is_a city [sacred to its people] Theseus forbids Hippolytus to return to Athens or to any shore where Theseus's arm is strong. Hippolytus bids farewell to the city of old Erechtheus as he leaves.

is_the_origin_of Phaedra [her ancestral homeland] Phaedra recalls her origins in Crete and refuses to shame the old proud Cretan castle through her conduct. The Chorus refers to the Cretan strand and to Phaedra's voyage from her joyous home to a distant marriage.

The castle, Pittheus's castle and royal residence, is Theseus's home in Trozên. After a hunt, Hippolytus and hunters enter while Phaedra is brought out; later it holds her bier and mourning handmaids, opens for Theseus, then closes behind him.

l: Phaedra's love for Hippolytus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Phaedra's secret, divinely caused passion for Hippolytus begins when she sees him in Athens. It wastes her away, drives her to fast and fear dishonor, and, despite her resistance and the Nurse's intervention, ends in her false accusation of him.

l: purity and innocence, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Purity is a virtue associated with freedom from human corruption. Hippolytus treats it as abstention from ordinary desire, offering Artemis a garland gathered by pure hands and claiming innocence; Phaedra doubts inner cleanliness, while Theseus rejects Hippolytus’s claim as proof.

l: honor and shame, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Honor and shame govern Phaedra’s choices: she values honor above survival, conceals love to turn shame into honor, resists comforting falsehood, and finally chooses death after exposure to preserve some honor for her husband, children, and family.

l: illness and suffering, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Phaedra's secret love appears as a wasting illness: she lies weak, refuses food, changes restlessly, and speaks in fevered images. The Nurse says that caring for another person's pain is harder than bearing one's own, and the women cannot initially identify the cause.

Death is the feared and desired end of Phaedra’s suffering, love, and disgrace: she imagines dying without thought or knowledge, while Aphrodite foresees it in her vengeance against Hippolytus. Phaedra says she will die soon, the Chorus expects hanging in the bridal room, and the Nurse discovers her caught in a noose. Theseus and the women call it a bitter calamity for the household.

The gods are powerful spirits whose favor and demands humans must respect: Aphrodite punishes Hippolytus, Artemis is honored and invoked, and all are bound by Zeus’s fixed will while bringing human error.
Hippolytus’s vehicle leaves Trozên in exile, overturns when its wheel catches a rock, entangles and drags him, and is broken against rocks.
Hippolytus's four-horse team panics at the Sea-Bull, resists control, crashes his chariot into rocks, and causes his fatal injuries.

Semele is a Theban princess, daughter of Cadmus, bride of Zeus, and mother of Dionysus. She dies when heavenly fire or lightning consumes her, leading to Dionysus’s unusual birth. Dionysus comes to Thebes to defend her reputation and prove that she bore a god. Her sacred tomb is in Pentheus’s Castle, where heavenly fire appears when Dionysus summons divine power.
Love, a powerful divine force, afflicts Phaedra with forbidden desire, blinding and wounding her; it brings joy and ruin, shame, and impending death despite resistance.

is_associated_with Phaedra [as both deed and suffering] Phaedra regards both the act and the suffering associated with her forbidden love as shameful. She fears that her shame will be exposed to others and believes that living with it would dishonour her husband, children, and household.

l: Phaedra's suicide by hanging, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Phaedra's suicide by hanging is her self-inflicted death in the Castle, intended to preserve her and her children's honour. After deciding to kill herself and considering how, she goes alone to her bridal room, ties a noose, and hangs herself; the women later see her body beneath the rafters.

are_destined_to_live_in Athens [as free and honourable men] Phaedra says that her children will one day live in ancient Athens as free, honourable men who can be proud of their mother. She fears that her disgrace would shame them and makes their future reputation one reason for choosing death.

Poseidon is Theseus’s father, invoked as a divine source of three prayers. When Theseus asks him to kill Hippolytus before day’s end or drive him into exile, Poseidon grants the prayer and sends the force that kills Hippolytus; Artemis says Theseus bears responsibility.

l: women of the household, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: form Chorus [as the women’s chorus] The women hear the Nurse's cries from within the Castle and debate whether to enter and loosen Phaedra's noose. They later mourn Phaedra, react with horror to Theseus's accusation, and lament the destruction of the King's household.

l: Theseus's accusation of Hippolytus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: claims Hippolytus's guilt [for violating Phaedra] After reading Phaedra's tablet, Theseus publicly declares that Hippolytus violently laid hands on his wife. He treats Phaedra's dead hand and the tablet as witnesses stronger than Hippolytus's oath.

l: Theseus's curse on Hippolytus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Theseus's curse on Hippolytus is a prayer to Poseidon, spoken by Theseus, demanding Hippolytus's death or friendless exile. Using one of Poseidon's three granted prayers, Theseus invokes the god; Poseidon fulfills it when terrified horses destroy Hippolytus, although Artemis calls the curse unrighteous because Hippolytus is innocent.

is_from Athens [imposed by Theseus] Theseus casts Hippolytus out of all his realms and commands him never to return to Athens or any land under Theseus's power. Hippolytus leaves reluctantly, asking his friends to give him god-speed and declaring that no man is more pure of spot.

contains Phaedra's accusation of Hippolytus [in writing] The tablet found with Phaedra is read by Theseus and becomes the basis of his accusation against Hippolytus. Theseus says it speaks clearly without requiring a prophet, while Hippolytus is not allowed to overturn its testimony.

l: Phaedra's accusation of Hippolytus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: accuses Hippolytus [of laying violent hands on Phaedra] Phaedra's written accusation is not quoted directly, but Theseus interprets the tablet as declaring that Hippolytus violated her. Hippolytus denies the charge and says that he cannot reveal the whole truth without breaking his oath.

l: truth and falsehood, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: are_contrasted purity and innocence [in the search for guilt] Theseus wishes that there were a test of love or distinct voices that could separate the true from the false and expose liars. Hippolytus insists that the sunlight and earth would witness his innocence, but Theseus treats the tablet as the clearer proof.

l: the gods' justice, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: is_questioned_by Chorus [because human deeds and rewards seem mismatched] The Chorus questions how human deeds can be matched with their rewards when good and evil repeatedly replace one another. Theseus sees Phaedra's death and the accusation against Hippolytus as part of divine anger, while Hippolytus's fate presents an apparent conflict between innocence, punishment, and the will of the gods.
A bondsman of Theseus, he rushes in to report Hippolytus's fatal chariot wreck, affirming Hippolytus's innocence and rejecting claims of sin.
A huge supernatural monster rises from the sea, terrifies and drives Hippolytus’s horses toward rocks, wrecks the chariot, then disappears.

is_caused_by the curse [the curse spoken by Theseus] Hippolytus's death results from the wreck of his chariot after the Sea-Bull terrifies his horses. Before dying, he forgives Theseus and is promised lasting honor by Artemis.
Hippolytus's chastity makes him reject Phaedra and refuse Cypris's worship. Artemis calls him saintly and true, while Cypris is said to hate him for his chastity.

Cadmus, founder and former king of Thebes, is the father of Semelê and Agave, husband of Harmonia, and maternal grandfather of Pentheus. He yields the throne to Pentheus, keeps Semelê’s tomb sacred, and supports Dionysus, urging Pentheus to honor him. After Pentheus’s destruction, Cadmus recovers his scattered body and helps Agave recognize him. Dionysus condemns Cadmus and his family: Cadmus and Harmonia go into exile, and he is destined to become serpent-like before reaching the Islands of the Blest with her.

Pentheus is a mortal king of Thebes, son of Agave and Echion and grandson of Cadmus. Ruling in Cadmus's stead, he rejects Dionysus's worship as impious and dangerous, refuses Dionysus offerings and prayers, and begins war against him. Hearing of women’s secret rites, Pentheus orders guards to seize them and the stranger teaching the worship, mocks Teiresias and Cadmus, and seeks to destroy the sanctuary. He has Dionysus bound and imprisoned, but after the castle is shaken he attacks a false image and believes the prisoner escaped. He then orders armed action against the wild women. Dionysus gradually controls Pentheus’s thoughts; though he resists, Pentheus is transformed and dressed as a Bacchanal in a robe, snood, fawn-skin, and with a wand. He goes to spy on the Bacchae, climbs a pine tree, and is exposed as their enemy. Agave, Ino, Autonoë, and the other Maenads tear him apart despite his plea that Agave recognize him. He dies as a consequence of this spying.

Agave, daughter of Cadmus and mother of Pentheus, leads one band of wild women on Kithaeron. As a Bacchanal hunter, she awakens the women with the god’s cry, directs worship, and joins attacks on cattle and villages. In ecstatic Bacchic frenzy, she carries out Pentheus’s foretold punishment, kills him, and returns carrying his head on a wand while believing it is a lion’s. When Cadmus restores her recognition, she understands that she and her sisters killed Pentheus and that Dionysus punished their house. She is then exiled with her sisters from Thebes.

Teiresias, an old blind prophet, supports Dionysus in Bacchic dress, joins Cadmus in worship, defends the god’s power, warns Pentheus that resistance is madness, and departs to continue serving Dionysus.

The Bacchae is a play associated with Dionysus’s worship, dances, rites, and women dwelling in the mountains and following his religious movement; it was first produced after Euripides’s death with Iphigenia in Aulis and Alcmaeon.

Thebes is a Hellenic city and land, first visited by Dionysus to establish his worship. It contains the Tomb of Semelê beside the Castle of Pentheus, the royal hall, and has the Wall of Seven Gates. Nursed by Semelê, it is ruled by Pentheus, whose impiety rejects Dionysus. Dionysus expels its women under his magic; their wild actions bring destruction to Thebes and surrounding settlements as Pentheus prepares for war. Pentheus leaves the city disguised and, in madness, sees Thebes and its wall doubled. The city suffers until it recognizes Dionysus, and the royal house ends disgraced as Agave and Cadmus depart.

Kithaeron is a mountain region associated with wild women and Bacchic rites. Its cattle graze there while the women sleep, worship Dionysus, perform wonders, slaughter cattle, and attack nearby villages. Pentheus goes there to hide among pines and observe the Maenads, but Dionysus gives him to their vengeance; they tear apart and scatter his body through its ravines and woodland.

l: Castle of Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: is_destroyed_by the destruction of Pentheus's house [divine destruction] Pentheus's Castle is shaken by a powerful earthquake and struck by fire at Semele's tomb. Its structure is overthrown and left in ruins while Pentheus is inside.

l: Chorus of Inspired Damsels, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: The Chorus of Inspired Damsels is a chorus of Eastern Bacchic maidens who serve, worship, and follow Dionysus in ecstatic mountain rites. They come from Asia, awaken sacred music, and gather Thebes in song around Pentheus’s hall. Their songs praise Dionysus’s birth, powers, and worshippers; condemn Pentheus’s scorn; and seek justice while fearing for the city. Imprisoned by Pentheus, they escape without mortal aid, return freely to the woods, dance for Bromios, and invoke divine law, Justice, and Dionysus’s wrath.
The Eastern Women enter after Dionysus departs, wearing white robes and fawn-skins, carrying ritual instruments and thyrsi, then begin a mystic song of worship.

l: the Theban women, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: The Theban women are Dionysus’s Bacchic followers, driven from their homes to the hills and mountain, where they carry thyrsi, dance, pray, and perform secret rites. Though Pentheus alleges sexual wrongdoing, Teiresias says pure-hearted women need not be stained. Sleeping in bands on Kithaeron, they wake to worship, draw water, wine, milk, and honey from the earth, then display supernatural force: slaughtering cattle, defeating villagers, taking children, breaking metal, ravaging settlements, and remaining protected from harm.

Dionysian worship is a sacred divine service taught by Dionysus throughout the world, centered on his dances, rites, and mysteries. It is practiced by women in ecstatic mountain rites, including the Bacchic procession, dances, songs, music, prayer, sacrifice, wine, ivy crowns, fawn-skins, thyrsoi, timbrels, pipes, and sacred regalia. Its mysteries are restricted to chosen followers and reject sinners, while their emblems and benefits remain hidden from the uninitiated. Teiresias and Cadmus defend it as ancient and legitimate. Dionysus seeks Thebes’s recognition and participation in his divine rites.
Dionysus veils his godhead in mortal form while working to reveal himself as a true god. He warns that he will personally defend his followers if Thebes attacks them.

Dionysus's birth is attributed to Zeus and Semelê. Semelê's sisters deny this account and claim that she falsely invoked Zeus to conceal human shame, but Dionysus says he has come to prove the truth of his birth.

l: Pentheus's war against Dionysus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Pentheus's war against Dionysus consists of rejecting Dionysus's person and refusing him drink-offerings and prayers. Dionysus responds by declaring that Pentheus and Thebes will face his power.

The thyrsus is a sacred wand of Dionysian worship, belonging to Dionysus and later taken by Pentheus. Dionysus gives Pentheus one and teaches him to carry and swing it like the Bacchae. In the Messenger’s account, wild women use such wands to draw water, produce wine, and defeat armed men.
The dappled fawn-skin is one of the items Dionysus prescribes for Pentheus's disguise. Pentheus accepts the costume despite his earlier refusal to wear a woman's robe.

The mountain is a place of Dionysian worship, where Bacchic maidens gather for dancing, prayer, revelry, and visions. As Pentheus sends men to hunt them and spies there under Dionysus’s lead, the Chorus calls for divine judgment.

l: the Bacchic procession, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: The Bacchic procession, led by Dionysus toward the hills, carries Theban women from homes and looms; imagined as joyful, music-filled ecstatic dancing, it moves from mountains into streets, towns, and towers, summoning Dionysus.

l: Pentheus's persecution of Dionysus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: is_carried_out_by Pentheus's bodyguard [under Pentheus's orders] Pentheus's persecution begins when he orders the arrest of Dionysian worshippers and commands his guards to seek the girl-faced stranger who has introduced the rites. He also orders Teiresias's sanctuary to be wrecked and threatens the stranger with imprisonment, judgment, and death.

l: forgetting and release from care, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Teiresias says that Dionysus's wine rests the spirit from grieving and allows people to forget the burdens of the day in sleep. The Chorus likewise associates the god with the vanishing of care, the forgiveness of hate, and a crownèd slumber after divine and human feasts.

is_a devotees of Dionysus [Bacchic worshippers] The Chorus laments Dionysus's imprisonment and calls on him to oppose Pentheus. It praises Dionysus as a god and rejoices when the earthquake and fire reveal his power. After Dionysus returns, the Chorus welcomes him and urges Pentheus to honor him.

The Messenger returns from Kithaeron and reports that the wild women have performed miraculous acts, slaughtered cattle, defeated armed villagers, and ravaged nearby settlements. He urges Pentheus to accept Dionysus and warns that destroying the god would destroy joy and love.

shakes Pentheus's Castle [divine manifestation] The earthquake is summoned by Dionysus's voice and shakes the pillars of Pentheus's Castle. It accompanies the god's release and the overthrow of Pentheus's house.

l: the fire from heaven, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: burns Semele [at her tomb] The fire from heaven is identified with the blaze that once came upon Semele. It rises from Semele's tomb and burns against Pentheus's house when Dionysus calls upon it.

l: the destruction of Pentheus's house, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: is_caused_by Dionysus [through divine power] Pentheus's house is destroyed after the earthquake and fire strike it. Dionysus says that the house lies in wreck as a sign of Pentheus's punishment for opposing the god.

l: the slaughter of the cattle, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: is_carried_out_by the wild women [during their mountain rites] The wild women attack the herds on the mountain and tear the cattle apart with their bare hands. Bulls and cows are dismembered, with ribs, limbs, and flesh scattered through the air and among the pine branches.
Women followers of Dionysus worship him; his chosen discover Pentheus, who is then carried away by them.

Maenads are wild Maids of God and followers of Dionysus, inhabiting mountains in sacred, ecstatic revels and defending holy mysteries. On Kithaeron, they are called to rage against Pentheus; after he rejects Dionysus and spies in woman’s guise, they pull down his pine tree, pursue him, and tear him apart.

is_a wild Maids [possessed by divine worship] Pentheus intends to spy upon the Bacchanals and fears that they will triumph over him. He is dressed like one of them before setting out toward the mountain.
The hills are described as the place of the Chosen's delight and the Bacchae's worship. Pentheus wants to see the women praying on them.

l: the long dances, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: is_a Bacchic revelry [desired by the maidens] The long dances are remembered by the Maidens as dances continuing through the dark until the stars wane. They are associated with dew, wind, running feet, and freedom in the wild lands.
Bacchic madness overshadows Pentheus after Dionysus dresses him. It clouds his reason, makes him see doubled sights and horns on Dionysus, and fills him with excited, violent, and deluded thoughts.

is_a Bacchic madness [mental condition] Pentheus's transformation changes him from a resisting king into a figure dressed as a Bacchanal. He accepts the robe, snood, fawn-skin, and wand, loses power over his own mind, and leaves to spy on the Bacchae.

is_a ordeal [presided over by Dionysus] Pentheus's trial is presented as the ordeal awaiting him when he enters the Bacchae's domain. Dionysus says that Pentheus will be carried away and that only God and Dionysus can pass the ordeal unscathed.
Pentheus's death, foretold by Dionysus as a lasting sign, is divine justice for opposing him. It occurs when, at Dionysus's command, the Maenads pull down Pentheus's pine tree and tear him apart.
is_a trap [for Pentheus] Dionysus declares that the lion is walking into the net. The image describes Pentheus entering the trap prepared for him as he goes to spy on the Bacchae.

is_a freedom from fear [as defined by the Chorus] Wisdom is presented as freedom from fear, the ability to breathe and wait, and the refusal to answer hatred with hatred. The Chorus asks what else Wisdom can be besides this release from striving.

is_a eternal order [unchanging and nature-born] The Chorus describes an abiding law that is not made by human striving and that remains strong through the ages. It condemns Pentheus for acting in defiance of such law.

Justice is the visible wrath of the Lord against the impious: summoned with a lifted sword against Pentheus, it punishes his tyrannous, lawless denial and mockery of Dionysus and brings suffering upon Cadmus's family.

l: Wrath of the Lord, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: punishes the tyrannous [through divine retribution] The Chorus calls for the Wrath of the Lord to come visibly for doom and deed. It asks that Pentheus be struck until his throat and heart bleed.

is_loved for ever [as a principle of wisdom] The Chorus asks whether Loveliness should not be loved forever. Loveliness is associated with divine grace, freedom from fear, and the beautiful life of the wild lands.

awaits the proud [patiently and inevitably] God's judgment is said to wait for those who worship the Ruthless Will and for proud dreams that make things greater without God. The Chorus presents it as slow but unfailing.

l: the Spirit of God, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: is_a eternal law [strong and unchanging] The Spirit of God is described as the enduring law that remains strong through the ages. The Chorus says that human plans and efforts are vain when they strive beyond its laws.

reports Pentheus's death [to the Leader and Chorus] The Messenger reports Pentheus's death on Kithaeron. He describes how Dionysus bent a pine tree for Pentheus to climb, revealed him to the Maenads, and how Agave and the others tore him apart.

participate_in the tearing apart of Pentheus [during Bacchic frenzy] Cadmus' daughters, including Agave, Ino, and Autonoë, are driven into a Dionysian frenzy on Kithaeron. They seize Pentheus and participate in his dismemberment, bringing ruin upon their family.

Pentheus's head is carried from Kithaeron by Agave, who mistakes it for the head of a lion and intends to display it on the palace. Cadmus makes her look at it until she recognizes it as the head of her son.

is_a murdered body [found scattered in Kithaeron's woodland] Pentheus's body is found by Cadmus after a difficult search through Kithaeron. It has been torn limb from limb, and Cadmus carries its remains back to Thebes on a bier.
Bacchic frenzy possesses Agave and drives Cadmus' daughters to Kithaeron, where the women mistake Pentheus for a wild beast and attack him; it later clears when Cadmus reveals the head Agave carries.

l: the hunt on Kithaeron, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: The hunt on Kithaeron is presented by Agave as a triumphant capture of a lion, though the supposed prey is Pentheus. It is actually the divinely directed pursuit that leads to his death and dismemberment.

l: the tearing apart of Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: occurs_at Kithaeron [in the mountain wilderness] The tearing apart of Pentheus is carried out by Agave, Ino, Autonoë, and the Maenads. His arms, legs, flesh, and other parts are scattered through the mountain woodland, while Agave carries away his head.

l: truth and recognition, Hippolytus; The Bacchae
s: Truth and recognition emerge when Cadmus leads Agave from her belief that she carries a lion's head to the knowledge that it is Pentheus's head. Her recovery of memory and understanding transforms her triumph into grief and reveals the reality of the slaughter.
